report:
## Conclusion

The claim is well supported by high-quality evidence: add-on cannabidiol (CBD, as the pharmaceutical formulation Epidiolex) reduces convulsive seizure frequency in children with Dravet syndrome, though it comes with a meaningfully higher rate of side effects.

**Primary evidence.** The pivotal double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Devinsky et al., NEJM 2017) randomized 120 children/young adults with drug-resistant Dravet syndrome to CBD (20 mg/kg/day) or placebo added to existing therapy. Median convulsive-seizure frequency fell from 12.4 to 5.9 per month with CBD versus 14.9 to 14.1 with placebo—a statistically significant treatment effect—but CBD was associated with more adverse events, mainly diarrhea, vomiting, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618).

A follow-up dose-ranging RCT (JAMA Neurology, GWPCARE2) confirmed that both 10 and 20 mg/kg/day doses produced clinically relevant seizure reductions, with the lower dose showing better tolerability (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458). Long-term open-label extension data (Epilepsia, 2019/2021) showed sustained median reductions of roughly 45–74% in convulsive seizures over follow-up up to three years, supporting durability of effect (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/epi.14628).

**Caveats.** Broader systematic reviews/meta-analyses of CBD across epilepsy syndromes note consistent efficacy signals but also consistently elevated adverse-event risk (GI symptoms, somnolence, liver enzyme elevation), and call for more long-term comparative safety data (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10787-024-01523-x).

**Bottom line:** Multiple independent RCTs and long-term extensions support that add-on CBD reduces convulsive seizures in Dravet syndrome; the effect is real but modest, and benefits must be weighed against a nontrivial side-effect burden.
